examples.label: OSCP Ch12 — find exploit-category NSE scripts (discover usable exploit scripts)
OSCP Ch12 — read an NSE script's description before running it (OSCP Ch12 B17)

notes: Service/version detection (-sV) probes open ports with service-specific payloads. Combine with -sC for default scripts. Use --version-intensity 0-9 to trade speed for accuracy. Results feed directly into searchsploit and vulnerability lookups. OSCP Ch12 workflow: grep Exploits /usr/share/nmap/scripts/*.nse to list exploit-category scripts; nmap --script-help=<name>.nse to verify what a script actually does before running it (important: some NSE 'exploit' scripts are destructive). Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 12 (Locating Public Exploits).

recommended.note: Look up exploits for the versions found.

name: Nmap - Service Scanning
description: The standard enumeration scan: all ports, version detection, and default scripts. Narrow with per-port script scans once you see what's open.

defense.why_it_works: Service/version scanning probes each open port and matches the responses against a signature database to identify the exact software and version running — the basis for CVE matching and targeted exploitation.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to the target and previously identified open ports.
defense.impact: A precise service-and-version inventory, enabling targeted exploit selection.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for execution of network enumeration utilities (nmap, netcat, net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, particularly when chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands. [AN1584] Sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands issued from bash scripts or interactive shells to map remote hosts are a strong behavioral indicator.
defense.artifacts: A burst of connections across many ports plus version-probe payloads in IDS/firewall logs; a scan pattern detectable by IDS.
defense.prevention:
A firewall that restricts which source addresses can reach service ports will cause Nmap to report those ports as 'filtered' rather than 'open', preventing version enumeration on restricted services.

[MITRE T1046 M1042] Disable or remove unnecessary services and functionality that expose attack surface. [M1030] Implement network segmentation to limit the set of hosts reachable from any given compromised system. Use firewalls to restrict which source addresses can reach each service port.
defense.evasion: Slow the scan (-T0/-T1), use decoys (-D) to bury the real source among spoofed ones, fragment packets (-f), or spoof the source port (--source-port 53) to evade rate-based IDS and simple firewall rules — these dedicated evasion techniques are covered in depth in the Nmap module.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces — should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services
